content.title: About
content.content: Salsa, pico de gallo is a fresh Mexican sauce made from finely diced tomatoes, onion, chili pepper, cilantro, lime juice, and salt. It has a bright, slightly spicy flavor and a crunchy texture, perfect as a dip or a topping for dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pico de gallo literally means “little rooster’s beak,” but in cooking it refers to finely chopped ingredients.
Traditionally the salsa is uncooked, preserving maximum vitamins and aromas.
There are many regional variations that differ by type of pepper and may include fruits like mango.
Salsa is commonly served with tortillas, tacos, guacamole, and used as a meat marinade.
In the United States salsa has become the most popular condiment in fast‑food restaurants, surpassing ketchup.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes and lime provide vitamin C, which supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Salsa is low in calories, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes has anti‑inflammatory properties and supports heart health.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Cilantro and lime add flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Capsaicin from chili peppers stimulates gastric juice production and aids digestion.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tomatoes, onion, or chili peppers.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: Very hot salsa can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt intake may raise blood pressure; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: If left at room temperature too long, salsa can develop bacterial growth; follow storage guidelines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use salsa as a dip for chips, tortillas, or raw vegetables, add it to tacos, burritos, salads, marinate meat, or serve it with fish and seafood. Adjust the heat level by adding more or less chili to suit your taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store salsa in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze in small portions; after thawing, stir as the texture may change.
